titulo.texto: Templo Mayor and Its Museum: The Heart of Tenochtitlan

frase_gancho.texto: Next to the Cathedral stood the center of the Mexica universe, and its remains now coexist with the city that grew on top of it.

puente_narrativo.texto: Walk a few steps toward the plaza that opens next to the museum entrance. It is the [Plaza del Seminario](cdmx_35_plaza_seminario), and here history peeks out onto the street.

como_llegar.texto: Go around the Cathedral along its eastern side to Seminario Street, where the ruins of the Templo Mayor await you.

guion_corto.texto: It grew to measure about eighty meters on each side and about forty-five meters in height. That is how large the Templo Mayor was in its final stage. It was the most important building in Tenochtitlan. At its summit stood two shrines, one for Huitzilopochtli, god of war, and another for Tláloc, god of rain. In fifteen twenty-one the city fell, and the capital of New Spain was laid out over its ruins. The temple lay buried for centuries. The modern search picked up speed in nineteen seventy-eight, when workers from the Light Company came across an enormous circular stone. Since then, the excavation and the site museum have told the story of what this ceremonial heart was like.

guion_largo.texto:
You are standing in the heart of what was Tenochtitlan. According to tradition, the Mexica arrived at a small island in Lake Texcoco around thirteen twenty-five, guided by their god Huitzilopochtli. From that island they built a city with landfill, canals, dikes and bridges. At the center they built the Templo Mayor, the most important work of Mexica society and the center of its religious universe.

The temple was not built all at once. Archaeologists distinguish seven construction stages, in addition to partial expansions. Each one was built over the previous one, like the layers of an onion. All of them kept two features: the double staircase and the two shrines at the summit. The one to the south belonged to Huitzilopochtli, god of war and the sun. The one to the north belonged to Tláloc, god of rain and fertility. The precinct covered a little more than a hectare.

One of the temple’s two halves had a story of its own. Fray Bernardino de Sahagún recorded that Huitzilopochtli was born on the Coatépetl, the hill of the serpent. He was born already armed, just as his sister Coyolxauhqui and his brothers were about to kill their mother, Coatlicue. He defeated Coyolxauhqui, beheaded her and hurled her body down the slope. The archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma maintains that the Templo Mayor gave material form to that story. Huitzilopochtli stood at the top and, at the foot of the staircase, the dismembered goddess.

The goddess reappeared on the twenty-first of February, nineteen seventy-eight. Workers from the then Light and Power Company were digging at the corner of Guatemala and Argentina when they came across a circular monolith. It was Coyolxauhqui, beheaded and dismembered, just as the myth tells it. The sculpture measures three meters twenty-five centimeters in diameter and weighs almost eight tons. The discovery gave rise to the Templo Mayor Project, founded by Matos Moctezuma. Between nineteen seventy-eight and nineteen eighty-two, more than seven thousand objects were recovered.

But the search went back a long way. The first archaeological finds in the city were recorded in seventeen ninety. In nineteen thirteen Manuel Gamio discovered the southwest corner of the temple, when people still believed it lay beneath the Cathedral. Archaeologists have located more than one hundred offerings, deposited by the Mexica during the different construction stages. In October of two thousand six, the monolith of Tlaltecuhtli, weighing almost twelve tons, appeared just a few steps away. After three years of restoration, it is displayed with its original polychromy in the museum’s lobby.

That is why the site museum exists, inaugurated on the twelfth of October, nineteen eighty-seven. It was designed by the architects Pedro Ramírez Vázquez and Javier Ramírez Campuzano. Its plan echoes the logic of the temple, with two wings of four halls each: one devoted to Huitzilopochtli and the other to Tláloc. The tour brings together the background of the research, tribute and trade, and flora and fauna. It also includes objects from the colonial period, when the Spanish city rose over the Mexica one. Among its best-known pieces is Coyolxauhqui herself.

Admission is paid and includes the archaeological zone and the museum. Check the current hours and closing days, because they may change. What you can see for free from the plaza already helps you understand the place, but if you decide to go in, set aside time to walk through it unhurriedly.

Think about the layers of time that come together here. Tenochtitlan falls in fifteen twenty-one, the viceregal city grows on top of it and, centuries later, archaeology brings back part of the sacred precinct. That precinct came to have seventy-eight buildings, and the Urban Archaeology Program has located forty-five of them, at least in part. That is why the [Cathedral](cdmx_27_catedral) and the [National Palace](cdmx_29_palacio_nacional) stand just a few steps from the Mexica remains.

texto.Period: Mexica Postclassic; the temple remained in use until 1521
texto.Museum: inaugurated October 12, 1987, designed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez and Javier Ramírez Campuzano

texto.pregunta: Myth: The Templo Mayor was discovered by pure chance in nineteen seventy-eight, and before that no one knew it was here.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The discovery of Coyolxauhqui was accidental, since it was made by workers from the Light and Power Company, but the first finds were recorded in seventeen ninety, and in nineteen thirteen Manuel Gamio had already discovered a corner of the temple.
